changes.before:
Conversations about race and public programs often stall because people are answering different questions. One person hears a question about character: did someone mean to treat people differently? Another person is describing a pattern in results that no single person created. Both questions matter. They call for different responses, so it helps to name which one is on the table before choosing what to do.

The intent question asks whether anyone treated a person differently because of race, color, national origin, disability or another protected trait. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds. The Minnesota Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination in public services and in employment. A concern about one employee's conduct is serious. It goes to the person or area responsible, such as the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division or Human Resources, which make formal determinations.

The effect question asks how a rule, default or resource works in practice for the people who must use it. A deadline, a mailing process, an English-only form or a weekday-only phone line can produce different results for different households, even when every employee applies it the same way. Some organizations use the terms institutional racism and structural racism for these patterns. In plain words, the terms point to rules and systems that produce unequal results over time, separate from any one person's motives.

Most of the influence DHS and DSD staff hold is over rules and processes. We write eligibility procedures, design notices, set hours, choose which data to collect, approve contracts and decide how quickly an appeal is heard. Training one employee cannot fix a procedure that produces unequal results no matter who carries it out. Changing the procedure can. When results differ and no one can point to a biased act, the useful next question is which rule, default or resource is producing the pattern, and who has the authority to change it.

Race Forward distinguishes institutional racism within an organization from structural racism across connected institutions and historical systems. These concepts direct attention beyond individual motives. A difference in outcomes is a reason to investigate; it does not by itself establish its cause or a legal violation.

Refer possible discrimination promptly through established channels while examining the process; do not wait for proof of intent or treat a team review as a substitute for required reporting.

changes.before:
A neutral rule is written without reference to race. A neutral result is something else: the rule works about equally well for everyone it touches. Unequal results often arise in the gap between the two. A rule meets people who arrive with different amounts of wealth, time, trust, transportation, documentation and prior experience with government. Those differences did not arise by accident.

Minnesota has a well-documented example. The University of Minnesota Libraries' Mapping Prejudice project has identified thousands of racial covenants in Minneapolis and Hennepin County. These were clauses written into property deeds to keep people who were not white from buying or living on the land. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis has described how covenants, federal redlining maps that marked neighborhoods of color as high risk, and federal mortgage insurance practices that largely excluded buyers of color combined to shape who could buy homes and build wealth. It also describes the freeway built through Saint Paul's Rondo neighborhood, a center of Black community life. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis has also reported that Minnesota's gap between white homeownership and homeownership among households of color and Native American households is among the largest in the nation. Minnesota Compass publishes current homeownership rates by race. Use the published numbers and their date rather than repeating a figure from memory.

Home equity is how many families pay for emergencies, education, care and a stable address. When some families were blocked from building wealth across generations, that history shows up today. It shows up in who can meet an asset limit, who has a fixed address for mail, who can take unpaid time off for a daytime appointment, and who has reason to be cautious with a government agency. None of this requires any present-day employee to act with bias. The rule simply lands on conditions that history produced.

For DHS and DSD work, the practical skill is to look at a rule and ask what it assumes about the person on the other side. Documentation requirements assume access to records. Mailed notices with short deadlines assume stable housing. English-only phone lines assume a language. A degree requirement for a position assumes one path through education. Some requirements are necessary and set by law; others are habits. Separating the two is work that leaders and program staff can do, and any change applies to everyone who must meet the requirement.
changes.after:
A neutral rule is written without reference to race. That describes its wording, not whether it is justified, accessible or lawful. Examine how it works for the people affected and what explains any differences. A rule meets people who arrive with different amounts of wealth, time, trust, transportation, documentation and prior experience with government. Historical policies can shape those conditions, alongside other influences that require examination.

Minnesota has a well-documented example. The University of Minnesota Libraries' Mapping Prejudice project has identified thousands of racial covenants in Minneapolis and Hennepin County. These were clauses written into property deeds to keep people who were not white from buying or living on the land. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis has described how covenants, federal redlining maps that marked neighborhoods of color as high risk, and federal mortgage insurance practices that largely excluded buyers of color combined to shape who could buy homes and build wealth. It also describes the freeway built through Saint Paul's Rondo neighborhood, a center of Black community life. In its 2021 article, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis reported that Minnesota's gap between white homeownership and homeownership among households of color and Native American households was among the largest in the nation at that time. Minnesota Compass publishes current homeownership rates by race. Use the published numbers and their date rather than repeating a figure from memory.

Housing wealth and stability can affect a family’s resources for care, transport and responding to public agencies. Historical exclusion therefore provides context for examining present barriers. It does not tell you a particular household’s resources, trust or preferences. For example, ask whether a mailing rule reaches people with changing addresses and whether the records support that explanation. Asset rules vary by program and may exclude certain property; do not infer eligibility or hardship from race or homeownership.

For DHS and DSD work, the practical skill is to look at a rule and ask what it assumes about the person on the other side. Documentation requirements assume access to records. Mailed notices with short deadlines assume stable housing. English-only phone lines assume a language. A degree requirement for a position assumes one path through education. Some requirements are necessary and set by law; others are habits. Separating the two is work that leaders and program staff can do, and approved alternatives should follow clear standards. Individual accommodations and other lawful exceptions may also be required; identical treatment is not the only way to provide fair access.

Disparate impact is a legal idea leaders should understand at a working level, including how it changed. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds. For decades, federal Title VI regulations also reached criteria or methods of administration with discriminatory effects. The United States Department of Justice removed those provisions effective December 10, 2025. The United States Department of Health and Human Services, which funds DHS, removed its parallel provisions effective July 24, 2026. As of October 2026, both departments say Title VI prohibits only intentional discrimination and that they will not pursue disparate-impact liability. Both also say data on unequal outcomes can still help prove intentional discrimination. Whether other federal or Minnesota law reaches a given practice is a question for legal counsel.

The earlier analysis asked three questions. First, is there an adverse effect: does a specific policy cause a harm that falls disproportionately on one group? Second, is there a substantial legitimate justification: is the policy necessary to meet an important goal, supported by evidence rather than speculation? Third, is there a less discriminatory alternative that would meet the same goal for everyone?

Those questions no longer describe federal Title VI enforcement. You can still use them as a design discipline, because a careful program team asks them anyway: What is the effect? Why do we need this? Is there another way? What you should not do is announce a legal conclusion. Whether a practice violates Title VI, the Minnesota Human Rights Act or any other law is a formal determination for legal counsel, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, or an enforcement agency. Your job in a program review is to surface the pattern, document the reasoning and route concerns to the person or area responsible.

Data is where many reviews go wrong. Public sources such as Minnesota Compass, Minnesota Department of Health reports and DHS program dashboards can show differences by race and ethnicity. They cannot, on their own, tell you why a difference exists. Before using a number, check its date, its definitions, which groups were combined, how small the counts are, and whether data is missing more often for some groups. A combined category can hide large differences between, for example, Somali, Hmong, Karen and Ethiopian Minnesotans. Small numbers can swing sharply from year to year. Never invent or estimate a figure to make a point, and always cite where a number came from.

Numbers describe patterns; people describe how the pattern is lived. The Equity Analysis Toolkit pairs data and evidence with engagement for this reason. Talk with the people and partners affected, including counties and Tribal Nations where they administer services, about what the process is like from their side. Their account often points to the cause that the data only hints at.

Do not invent a figure or present an unsupported estimate as fact. Published estimates may be appropriate when their method, uncertainty and source are clear. Protect small groups from identification and use approved disclosure controls.

changes.before:
The State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit gives agencies a structured way to examine who a decision affects. Its quick guide works through impact assessment, partner engagement, data and evidence, access and accessibility, monitoring and evaluation, resources, and implementation and accountability. Its core questions are plain. What outcomes do we intend? Who are we including? How can we collaborate? What impact will result? How will we be accountable? How will we communicate?

The toolkit is only as strong as the map of authority you bring to it. Institutions repeat what they do not examine, and defaults last because they work for the people who set them. So for each part of a policy, ask who decided it, who can change it and who bears the cost if it stays. Some features are set by federal or state law. Others are set by DHS policy, by a division, by a contract, or by a supervisor's habit. Mapping decision rights keeps a review from ending in recommendations that no one has the authority to act on.

Habits deserve the same attention as rules. Ideas about what counts as professional communication, a reasonable pace, credible evidence or appropriate expertise often reflect the habits of the people who set the rule. Those habits get presented as a universal standard, and the mainstream default becomes the rule everyone is measured against. Naming this is a design observation, not an accusation. If a hiring panel treats one communication style as a sign of competence, written criteria tied to the job and applied to every candidate are the fix. If a stakeholder meeting assumes everyone can attend on a weekday afternoon, offering another time or a written option opens it to everyone.

Finally, connect the analysis to a decision with an owner. A review that produces a thoughtful document and no change has not done its job. Choose what to change (the rule, the default or the resource), who will do it, when you will look again, and how you will tell the people who informed the review what happened. The toolkit stresses action and continued reassessment. Expect the first change to reveal a second problem, and treat that as progress rather than failure.

Its quick guide works through impact assessment, partner engagement, data and evidence, access and accessibility, monitoring and evaluation, resources, and implementation and accountability. Its core questions are plain. What outcomes do we intend? Who are we including? How can we collaborate? What impact will result? How will we be accountable? How will we communicate?

The toolkit is only as strong as the map of authority you bring to it. Institutions repeat what they do not examine, and defaults last because they work for the people who set them. So for each part of a policy, ask who decided it, who can change it and who bears the cost if it stays. Some features are set by federal or state law. Others are set by DHS policy, by a division, by a contract, or by a supervisor's habit. Mapping decision rights keeps a review from ending in recommendations that no one has the authority to act on.

Habits deserve the same attention as rules. Ideas about what counts as professional communication, a reasonable pace, credible evidence or appropriate expertise often reflect the habits of the people who set the rule. Those habits get presented as a universal standard, and the mainstream default becomes the rule everyone is measured against. Naming this is a design observation, not an accusation. If a hiring panel treats one communication style as a sign of competence, review the selection methods with HR and use approved, job-related criteria with appropriate accommodations. Finally, connect the analysis to a decision with an owner. A completed review records a supported decision: retain the practice, revise it, test an authorized alternative, or seek further review. Explain why, identify who can act, and set a follow-up date. Tell participants what was decided and what remains unresolved. The toolkit stresses action and continued reassessment. Monitor benefits and unintended harms after a change. A newly discovered barrier calls for a response; it is not automatically evidence of success.
